subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Heart embryology: embryonic structures and derivatives
vignette: During a cardiac embryology tutorial, students are asked to identify the venous structure of the primitive heart that ultimately drains myocardial venous blood into the right atrium in the adult.
question: Which of the following adult structures is derived from the left horn of the sinus venosus?

options.text: Superior vena cava
Smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum)
Inferior vena cava
Coronary sinus
Smooth part of the left atrium

explanation_correct: The left horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to the coronary sinus, which drains venous blood from the myocardium into the right atrium. Its counterpart, the right horn of the sinus venosus, gives rise to the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum).

explanation_incorrect.A: The superior vena cava is derived from the right common cardinal vein and the right anterior cardinal vein, not from the sinus venosus horn.
explanation_incorrect.B: The smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) derives from the right horn of the sinus venosus, not the left horn.
explanation_incorrect.C: The inferior vena cava derives from the posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins.
explanation_incorrect.E: The smooth part of the left atrium derives from the primitive pulmonary vein.

educationalObjective: The left horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to the coronary sinus, while the right horn forms the smooth part of the right atrium.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Heart embryology: embryonic structures and derivatives
vignette: A student reviewing the embryologic regions of the primitive heart tube notes that one region of the early tube lies between the primitive ventricle and the truncus arteriosus and contributes to the walls of both mature ventricles.
question: Which of the following adult structures is derived from the bulbus cordis?

options.text: Smooth parts (outflow tract) of the left and right ventricles
Trabeculated parts of the left and right ventricles
Trabeculated parts of the left and right atria
Smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum)
Ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk

explanation_correct: The bulbus cordis gives rise to the smooth parts (outflow tract) of the left and right ventricles. In contrast, the primitive ventricle gives rise to the trabeculated parts of the ventricles, and the truncus arteriosus gives rise to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

explanation_incorrect.B: The trabeculated parts of the ventricles derive from the primitive ventricle, not the bulbus cordis.
explanation_incorrect.C: The trabeculated parts of the atria derive from the primitive atrium.
explanation_incorrect.D: The smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) derives from the right horn of the sinus venosus.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk derive from the truncus arteriosus, which lies distal to the bulbus cordis in the heart tube.

educationalObjective: The bulbus cordis gives rise to the smooth outflow parts of the left and right ventricles.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Heart embryology: embryonic structures and derivatives
vignette: A first-year medical student is constructing a table matching embryonic cardiac structures to their adult derivatives. She has correctly assigned the primitive atrium to the trabeculated parts of both atria but cannot recall the origin of the smooth-walled portion of the left atrium.
question: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the smooth part of the left atrium?

options.text: The left horn of the sinus venosus
The right horn of the sinus venosus
The bulbus cordis
The endocardial cushion
The primitive pulmonary vein

explanation_correct: The primitive pulmonary vein gives rise to the smooth part of the left atrium. The trabeculated parts of the left and right atria, by contrast, derive from the primitive atrium.

explanation_incorrect.A: The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes the coronary sinus, which drains into the right atrium.
explanation_incorrect.B: The right horn of the sinus venosus becomes the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum), not the left atrium.
explanation_incorrect.C: The bulbus cordis gives rise to the smooth outflow parts of the ventricles, not to atrial tissue.
explanation_incorrect.D: The endocardial cushion gives rise to the atrial septum, the membranous interventricular septum, and the AV and semilunar valves.

educationalObjective: The primitive pulmonary vein forms the smooth part of the left atrium; the primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of both atria.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Heart embryology: embryonic structures and derivatives
vignette: A radiologist reads a chest CT in a patient with an incidentally noted persistent left superior vena cava and begins reviewing which embryonic cardinal veins normally persist to form the definitive systemic venous drainage of the head and upper extremities.
question: Which of the following embryonic structures gives rise to the superior vena cava?

options.text: Posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins
Left horn of the sinus venosus
Right common cardinal vein and right anterior cardinal vein
Right horn of the sinus venosus
Truncus arteriosus

explanation_correct: The superior vena cava is derived from the right common cardinal vein and the right anterior cardinal vein. The paired cardinal venous systems otherwise largely regress; their asymmetric persistence explains why the SVC forms on the right and why a persistent left SVC can occur as a venous variant.

explanation_incorrect.A: The posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins give rise to the inferior vena cava, not the SVC.
explanation_incorrect.B: The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes the coronary sinus.
explanation_incorrect.D: The right horn of the sinus venosus becomes the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum).
explanation_incorrect.E: The truncus arteriosus is an arterial structure that gives rise to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

educationalObjective: The SVC derives from the right common cardinal and right anterior cardinal veins; the IVC derives from the posterior, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Heart embryology: embryonic structures and derivatives
vignette: While studying for an embryology exam, a student lists the derivatives of the endocardial cushion and must verify which structure on her list does not belong, since one of the listed structures derives from a different embryonic region of the heart tube.
question: Which of the following structures does NOT derive from the endocardial cushion?

options.text: Membranous interventricular septum
Smooth parts (outflow tract) of the left and right ventricles
Mitral valve
Atrial septum
Aortic valve

explanation_correct: The endocardial cushion gives rise to the atrial septum, the membranous interventricular septum, and the AV and semilunar valves. The smooth parts (outflow tract) of the ventricles instead derive from the bulbus cordis, so that structure does not belong on the endocardial cushion derivative list.

explanation_incorrect.A: The membranous interventricular septum does derive from the endocardial cushion, whose growth contributes to the membranous portion of the interventricular septum.
explanation_incorrect.C: The mitral valve derives from the fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal.
explanation_incorrect.D: The atrial septum derives in part from the endocardial cushion, toward which septum primum grows during atrial septation.
explanation_incorrect.E: The aortic valve derives from the endocardial cushions of the outflow tract.

educationalObjective: Endocardial cushion derivatives are the atrial septum, membranous interventricular septum, and AV and semilunar valves; the smooth ventricular outflow parts come from the bulbus cordis.
